passage:
I've taught at the pottery studio for eleven years, and I still remember the Thursday Bhavna almost walked out for good. She had been trying to centre clay on the wheel for six weeks. That day the lump wobbled off-centre for the fifth time, and she slapped it flat and said, 'I'm clearly not built for this, Minakshi.' Her jaw was tight; she was already untying her apron.
I didn't tell her to try harder. She had been trying hard, too hard. I pulled out the shelf of her first bowls, lopsided and cracked, and set them next to Tuesday's cup. She went quiet. Then I cut her clay into small balls, the size of an orange, and said, 'For two weeks, only centre. No pots. Stop after each one.'
She stayed. Last month she sold her first set of cups at the studio fair.

qa.q: How long had Bhavna been trying to centre clay on the wheel?
qa.a: Bhavna had been trying to centre clay on the wheel for six weeks.

qa.q: What does Bhavna's tight jaw and untying her apron suggest she was feeling?
qa.a: They suggest anger and defeat, and that she had nearly decided to give up pottery that day.

qa.q: Which two moves by Minakshi kept Bhavna going, and why did they work?
qa.a: Minakshi showed her first lopsided bowls next to her newer cup, and changed the practice to small balls and centring only, which gave proof of progress and a smaller, clearer task.

qa.q: What would change if Minakshi had simply said 'try harder'?
qa.a: Bhavna was already trying too hard, so more effort alone would likely have deepened her frustration and she might have left the studio.

grounding: It shows a mentor watching a student nearly quit, reminding her how far she had come and adjusting the practice rather than urging more effort.

passage:
Climbing club, coach's log, Saturday.
Eshaan (19) fell off the overhang problem on the blue wall eight times today. After the last fall he kicked the crash mat and said he was done with climbing, that he'd 'never be strong like Farhan'. He sat by the shoe rack for twenty minutes with his hood up.
I didn't give him the 'push through' speech. When he came to return his harness, I opened his first-week card on the noticeboard: he couldn't finish the easiest yellow route in June. He read it twice.
Then we changed the plan. No more full attempts on the blue problem this week. Only the heel-hook move, practised on the low traverse wall, five tries, then rest. He agreed to come Tuesday.
Next step: check on Tuesday whether the smaller drill feels doable, and keep his card where he can see it.
Chinmay

qa.q: How many times did Eshaan fall off the overhang problem today?
qa.a: Eshaan fell off the overhang problem on the blue wall eight times today.

qa.q: Why might Chinmay have held back the 'push through' speech after Eshaan kicked the mat?
qa.a: Chinmay seemed concerned that Eshaan felt defeated, and judged that reminding him of his progress would help more than pushing.

qa.q: What did Chinmay change at this stage, and why might it matter more than urging effort?
qa.a: Chinmay stopped his full attempts and gave him one heel-hook drill with rests, which turns a hopeless-looking problem into a small skill he can actually improve.

qa.q: How might Eshaan see his first-week card now?
qa.a: Seeing that he couldn't finish the easiest route in June may make him feel his effort has counted, which softens the sense that he is failing.

grounding: It shows a coach noticing a student's frustration and near-quitting, reminding him of his progress and adjusting his practice instead of pushing harder.

passage:
Vijay's coaching diary, 14 November
Zainab resigned three games in a row tonight, each time before the position was lost. After the third she pushed the pieces over and said, "I've been at this a year, sir. Kids of twelve beat me. I'm done."
My first instinct was the usual speech: study more, play more. I bit it back. She is already doing more; that's half the trouble. She plays forty blitz games a night and learns nothing from any of them.
So I pulled out her scoresheet from last January, the game where she lost her queen in eight moves. She stared at it and actually laughed.
Then we agreed on a change: no blitz for two weeks. One slow game a day, and afterwards she writes down the single move she regrets most. We'll go through them together on Fridays.
She left quieter. Not happy, but not quitting.

qa.q: How many blitz games does Zainab play a night?
qa.a: Forty blitz games a night.

qa.q: What was Vijay feeling when Zainab said she was done?
qa.a: He felt worried and tempted to lecture, but sensed that pushing for more effort would only deepen her frustration.

qa.q: Why is Vijay's change of practice a better turning point than urging harder work?
qa.a: Slow games and noting the one regretted move replace mindless blitz, so practice becomes focused instead of just longer.

qa.q: What is Zainab experiencing after the third resignation?
qa.a: She feels humiliated and angry, comparing herself with twelve-year-olds and convinced a year of work has gone nowhere.

grounding: A mentor sees a student about to quit, recalls how far she has come and changes the practice instead of demanding more effort.

Tejas: Before 10 pm? Bold, chhote bhai. What happened?
Hrithik: 3 hrs on one graph problem. wrong answer. again. everyone in my batch solved it in 20 mins
Hrithik: maybe coding just isn't for me
Tejas: Remember September? You couldn't write a loop without me checking it.
Tejas: Today you're arguing with graph problems. That's a big jump.
Hrithik: doesn't feel like it
Tejas: Fair. But three hours on the same attempt isn't practice, it's banging your head.
Tejas: New plan. 40 mins max per problem. Then read one solution, close it, and write it yourself tomorrow from memory.
Hrithik: feels like cheating
Tejas: It's how I learned. Send me tomorrow's attempt, I'll go through it with you 🙂
Hrithik: ok. not uninstalling. yet.

qa.q: How long did Hrithik spend on the graph problem?
qa.a: 3 hrs on one graph problem.

qa.q: What might Tejas be worried about when Hrithik says coding isn't for him?
qa.a: Tejas is worried that Hrithik's frustration will make him quit just before he improves, so he answers calmly instead of lecturing.

qa.q: Why is Tejas's new plan better than telling Hrithik to try harder?
qa.a: It caps time per problem and adds studying a solution, changing how he practises instead of piling on more frustrating hours.

qa.q: What is this stage like for Hrithik?
qa.a: Discouraging and lonely; he feels everyone in his batch is faster and reads each wrong answer as proof he doesn't belong in coding.

grounding: A senior mentor notices a student's frustration, reminds him of his progress and adjusts his practice so he does not quit.

passage:
In the potters' lane of the village, Ojas had watched Reena's pots collapse for nine days. Each time the clay rose past her wrist, the wall wobbled and folded like wet paper. Today she didn't even wait for it to fall. She stopped the wheel with her foot, pressed the clay into a lump and said, "Kaka, give my place to someone with better hands."
Ojas wiped his own hands slowly on his dhoti. Telling her to sit longer would not help; she was already first at the wheel every morning.
"Remember your first week? You couldn't centre the clay at all. Now you centre it before I finish my tea."
She shrugged, but her jaw loosened.
"Tomorrow, no tall pots," he said. "Only small bowls, and only the pulling-up part, slowly, twenty times. I'll sit beside you and watch your thumbs."

qa.q: For how many days had Reena's pots collapsed?
qa.a: Nine days.

qa.q: What was Ojas feeling as he wiped his hands slowly?
qa.a: He felt concerned and chose his words with care, knowing that urging her to sit longer would not help someone already working so hard.

qa.q: What turning point does Ojas create at this stage?
qa.a: He reminds Reena she can now centre clay easily, and changes the practice to small bowls and just the pulling-up step, with him beside her.

qa.q: What is Reena going through when she asks for her place to be given away?
qa.a: She feels defeated and embarrassed, sure that her hands are the problem after nine days of collapsing pots.

grounding: An older potter sees an apprentice near quitting, points to how far she has come and adjusts the practice rather than asking for more hours.

passage: At the climbing gym in Singapore, Tuan watched Selin fall off the purple route for the sixth time that evening, at exactly the same overhang. She dropped onto the mat, lay there and said to the ceiling, "I'm done. I'm clearly not built for this." Tuan had mentored her since she arrived three months ago, unable to reach the second hold on the easiest wall. He crouched beside the mat. "In March you couldn't finish the yellow wall. Tonight you warmed up on it." She didn't answer. "And you're not failing the route. You're failing one move, six times, while tired." He pointed at the overhang. "Tomorrow, fresh, we practise only that move from a low start. Ten tries, then home." Selin sat up slowly and looked at the purple holds as if seeing them for the first time.

qa.q: Where does Selin keep falling off the purple route?
qa.a: At exactly the same overhang.

qa.q: What might Tuan be worried about as Selin lies on the mat?
qa.a: Tuan is concerned she is about to quit at the hardest point, after three months of real progress.

qa.q: Why does Tuan's plan for tomorrow help more than urging her to try harder?
qa.a: It isolates the one move and practises it fresh, changing the practice instead of piling on tired attempts.

qa.q: How has Selin's view of the route changed by the end?
qa.a: She moves from feeling not built for climbing to seeing one learnable move, looking at it with fresh interest.

grounding: Shows a mentor watching a student nearly quit and helping by pointing to her progress and adjusting the practice rather than urging more effort.
